title: Sagrada Família towers: which ticket takes you up, and is it worth it?
subtitle: Two façades, one lift up, a long spiral down, and a church that is better from the inside.
excerpt: A ticket to the Sagrada Família does not include the towers. What a tower visit is, how the Nativity and Passion towers differ, who cannot go up, and when the basilica alone is the better choice.
longtail_phrases: is it worth going up the Sagrada Familia towers
Sagrada Familia Nativity or Passion tower which is better
does a Sagrada Familia ticket include the towers
can children go up the Sagrada Familia towers
how long does a visit to the Sagrada Familia take
meta_title: Sagrada Família towers: which ticket, and is it worth it?
meta_description: Basilica tickets do not include the towers. How the tower visit works, Nativity or Passion, who cannot go up, and when to skip it.

featured_image.alt: The towers of the Sagrada Família in Barcelona seen from the street, with a construction crane above them

content_html:
[place attraction="sagrada-familia" city="barcelona"]

The first stone of the Sagrada Família was laid on 19 March 1882, to the plans of another architect. Antoni Gaudí took the job over a year later, at thirty-one, and changed everything. He worked on the church for forty-three years, and for the last dozen on nothing else. In June 1926 he was struck by a tram on his way to evening prayers and died three days later. Of the eighteen towers he had drawn, exactly one was finished.

Ten years after that, in the first days of the Civil War, his workshop was set on fire and the plaster models he had left as instructions were smashed. The church you visit today was pieced together from the fragments, and it is still being built. Which leads to the question nearly every visitor asks at the moment of booking: the ticket with the towers, or without?

The Nativity façade, the only one Gaudí saw rise. Photo: Richard Mortel, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

What a tower visit actually is

Entry to the basilica and entry to the towers are two different things. A standard ticket lets you into the church, around its outside and into the small museum underneath. It does not take you up.

The tower visit is an extra, with its own time slot printed on the ticket, usually shortly after your entry time. A lift carries you up inside one tower. You step out high on the façade, cross to a neighbouring tower, look out through narrow stone openings, and then walk down: a long, tight spiral staircase with no landing to rest on and, on its inner side, an open well. There is no lift down.

The spiral staircase inside a tower: the way back to the ground. Photo: Tony Hisgett, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

You go up one façade or the other, never both on one ticket, and you choose which when you book.

Nativity or Passion?

  • The Nativity façade is the one built in Gaudí's lifetime, facing the sunrise. From its towers you are close to the carving he supervised himself, including the green ceramic cypress dotted with white doves between the spires, and a small bridge links two of the towers. The view runs over the grid of the Eixample towards the coast north of the centre.
  • The Passion façade, on the opposite side, was built from the 1950s onwards and its hard, angular sculptures were carved by Josep Maria Subirachs from the late 1980s. Its towers look the other way: over the city centre, towards the hill of Montjuïc and the port.

Neither is the wrong choice. If you care about Gaudí's own stonework, take the Nativity side. If you want the wider city view, take the Passion side.

Barcelona from a tower of the Nativity façade, framed by the stone of the church. Photo: Maksim Sokolov, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Is it worth it?

Be clear about what the towers are not. They are not a viewing platform: you look out through slits and from small balconies, and you spend more time on the stairs than at the openings. What you get is the building itself from close up, the mosaic pinnacles shaped like fruit, the scaffolding and the cranes, and the odd pleasure of walking down inside a stone spire.

What makes the Sagrada Família unlike any other church is inside, and every ticket includes it. The columns split into branches near the vault, like a stand of trees, and the stained glass is arranged by temperature: cool blues and greens on the side of the rising sun, oranges and reds on the side where it sets. On a clear day the stone changes colour by the hour.

The nave: columns that branch like trees, and coloured glass down both sides. Photo: Smiley.toerist, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

So: take the towers if you like heights, architecture seen from close up and a spiral staircase. Leave them out, without regret, if any of the following applies.

Who should not book the towers

  • Small children. The basilica has set a minimum age for the towers (six, at the time of writing), and older children must go up with an adult.
  • Anyone with vertigo, claustrophobia, a heart condition or knees that dislike a few hundred steps downwards.
  • Wheelchair users and anyone who cannot manage stairs: the way down has no alternative.
  • Anyone on a tight schedule on a day of wind or rain. The towers close in bad weather at short notice. The church visit goes ahead, the tower part does not.

What the partner's listings include

Read the titles slowly, because they sound more alike than they are.

  • "Fast track ticket" is entry to the basilica at a fixed time. Fast track means you do not queue to buy; everybody still passes the security check. No towers and no commentary unless the listing says so.
  • "Fast track ticket & audio tour" is the same entry plus a guide that plays in the partner's app on your own phone. Bring earphones.
  • "Audio tour" on its own is only the commentary. It does not get you through the gate, so you need an entry ticket from somewhere else.
  • A listing whose title mentions tower access. The partner sells a city audio walk bundled with a Sagrada Família ticket and names the towers in its title. Before you rely on it, open its "included" section and check that the towers are written there, and for which façade.

These are the tickets and audio tours our partner sells for the Sagrada Família, with today's prices:

[partner attraction="sagrada-familia" match="sagrada" limit="6"]

Booking and timing

  • Entry is for a fixed time and the popular hours sell out days ahead in high season. Do not plan on buying at the door.
  • For the light, go in mid-morning or in the last two hours before closing, when the low sun comes straight through the glass.
  • Allow an hour and a half for the basilica and the museum, and about half an hour more with a tower.
  • This is a working church with a dress code: covered shoulders, nothing see-through, shorts and skirts at least to mid-thigh, no swimwear.
  • The metro station Sagrada Família, on lines L2 and L5, is beside the church.

Hours change with the season and with services. The current ones are on our page for the Sagrada Família.

From here

Walk ten minutes up the Avinguda de Gaudí to the Hospital de Sant Pau, a whole Art Nouveau hospital by Gaudí's rival Lluís Domènech i Montaner. Gaudí's apartment buildings on the Passeig de Gràcia are about twenty-five minutes on foot in the other direction, and Park Güell is uphill, with a timed ticket of its own. For the rest, see what there is to do in Barcelona or build a route with the trip planner for Spain.

Cover photo: Américo Toledano, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: Does a Sagrada Família ticket include the towers?
faqs.a: No. A standard ticket covers the basilica and its museum. The towers are an extra with their own time slot, and it has to be chosen when you book.

faqs.q: Which Sagrada Família tower is better, Nativity or Passion?
faqs.a: The Nativity towers bring you close to the stonework built in Gaudí's lifetime. The Passion towers look over the city centre towards Montjuïc and the port. You visit one side only.

faqs.q: Do you have to walk down the Sagrada Família towers?
faqs.a: Yes. A lift takes you up, and the way down is a long, narrow spiral staircase. There is no lift down, so the towers are not suitable for people who cannot manage stairs.

faqs.q: Can children go up the Sagrada Família towers?
faqs.a: Small children cannot. The basilica sets a minimum age for the towers (six at the time of writing) and older children must be with an adult. Check the conditions when you book.

faqs.q: How long does a visit to the Sagrada Família take?
faqs.a: About an hour and a half for the basilica and the museum, and around two hours if you also go up a tower.

title: The Louvre in two hours: a route to the essentials without getting lost
subtitle: One entrance, three wings, and a single line through the museum that takes in what you came for.
excerpt: A two-hour route through the Louvre, stop by stop: the medieval fortress, the Venus de Milo, the Winged Victory, the Mona Lisa and the great French paintings, with the entrance to use and what each ticket includes.
secondary_keywords: what to see at the Louvre
longtail_phrases: how to see the Louvre in two hours
where is the Mona Lisa in the Louvre
which entrance to use at the Louvre
what to see at the Louvre besides the Mona Lisa
how not to get lost in the Louvre
meta_title: The Louvre in two hours: a route to the essentials
meta_description: A two-hour route through the Louvre: fortress, Venus de Milo, Winged Victory, Mona Lisa, the big French paintings. Which entrance, which ticket.

featured_image.alt: The Cour Carrée, the square courtyard of the Louvre palace, seen from an upper floor

content_html:
[place attraction="louvre" city="paris"]

On Monday 21 August 1911 the Louvre was closed for cleaning. An Italian workman called Vincenzo Peruggia, who had helped fit the museum's paintings with glass, lifted a small portrait off its hooks, took it out of its frame on a service staircase and walked into the street with it under his smock. Nobody noticed until the next day. The painting was gone for more than two years, and when the museum reopened, people queued to look at the empty space on the wall.

That theft, more than anything Leonardo did, made the Mona Lisa the most famous painting in the world. It also explains the modern Louvre: most visitors head for one room, get lost on the way, and leave tired, having seen a crowd. Two hours are enough to do much better, if you walk a line instead of wandering.

Why people get lost

The Louvre is a palace, not a building designed as a museum. It has three wings, Sully, Denon and Richelieu, which all start from the hall under the glass pyramid and meet again only in a few places. The floors do not always line up between wings, and around 35,000 works are on show. Nobody sees it all. The route below stays in Sully and Denon, where the best-known works are, and never doubles back.

Getting in

Entry is by timed ticket. Everybody passes a security check, with or without a ticket, so "skip the line" means the shorter line for people who already hold one. There are two usual ways in:

  • The Pyramid, in the main courtyard. The best-known entrance and the longest line.
  • The Carrousel du Louvre, the underground shopping gallery reached from 99 rue de Rivoli or straight from the metro station Palais Royal-Musée du Louvre (lines 1 and 7). Under cover, and often quicker.

Both bring you to the same hall under the pyramid. Leave coats and backpacks in the free lockers there, pick up a paper plan, and start with the escalator marked Sully.

The route, stop by stop

1. The medieval Louvre (Sully, lower level)

Before it was a palace, the Louvre was a fortress built around 1190 by King Philip Augustus to guard Paris from the west. Its moat and the base of its towers were dug out in the 1980s and you walk along them. Ten minutes, almost no crowd, and the building makes sense afterwards.

Under the museum: the walls of the fortress of about 1190. Photo: GFreihalter, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

2. The Venus de Milo (Sully, ground floor)

Go up one level and follow the signs to the Greek antiquities. The Venus was found by a farmer on the island of Milos in 1820 and reached the Louvre a year later. Walk around her: she was carved to be seen from every side.

The Venus de Milo, found on the island of Milos in 1820. Photo: Livioandronico2013, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

3. The Winged Victory of Samothrace (Denon, top of the Daru staircase)

From the Greek rooms you come out at the foot of a wide staircase, and the Victory stands at the top of it, on the prow of a stone ship, as she has since 1884. This is the best piece of staging in the museum. Stop halfway up the stairs, where the photograph is better than from the landing.

The Daru staircase, with the Winged Victory on its landing. Photo: Wilfredor, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

4. The Mona Lisa (Denon, first floor)

Turn right at the Victory and follow the flow into the largest room of the museum. The portrait is 77 centimetres high, behind thick glass and a barrier, and you will see it from a few metres away with phones raised around you. Give it five minutes, then turn round. On the opposite wall hangs Veronese's Wedding Feast at Cana, nearly ten metres wide, the biggest painting in the Louvre, and hardly anyone is looking at it.

5. The Grande Galerie and the big French paintings

Leave by the long gallery next door, lined with Italian painting, where other works by Leonardo hang with almost no one in front of them. Then cross to the two red rooms of very large French canvases: Delacroix's Liberty Leading the People, Géricault's Raft of the Medusa and David's Coronation of Napoleon, in which the painter put himself in the audience.

The Grande Galerie: Italian painting, and room to breathe. Photo: Cheng-en Cheng, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.

6. Michelangelo, on the way out (Denon, ground floor)

Take the stairs down to the Italian sculpture: Michelangelo's two Slaves, carved for the tomb of Pope Julius II, and Canova's Psyche Revived by Cupid's Kiss. From here the signs lead back to the pyramid.

That is two hours at a steady pace. If you have a third, spend it in the Richelieu wing, on the two glass-roofed sculpture courts and the apartments of Napoleon III.

What the tickets include

  • An entrance ticket is entry at a fixed time, nothing more. The route above is all you need to go with it.
  • A ticket with a highlights audio tour adds a guide in the partner's app on your own phone, with directions from room to room. It covers the permanent collection, not temporary exhibitions. Bring earphones.
  • A fast track ticket with hosted access adds a person who meets you and takes you in. Read exactly where the host leaves you: it is not a guided tour of the museum.
  • An audio tour "without a ticket" is commentary only. You still have to book your entry separately.

These are the Louvre tickets and audio tours our partner sells, with today's prices:

[partner attraction="louvre" match="louvre" limit="6"]

When to go

The museum is closed on Tuesdays. The first slot of the morning and the late-opening evenings are the calmest; the middle of the day is the worst, in every season. Visitors under 18 do not pay, but they need a reservation for a time slot like everyone else. Days, late evenings and room closures change, so check the current hours on our page for the Louvre before you set out.

From here

You come out into the Tuileries Garden, which runs west for a kilometre to the Place de la Concorde, with Monet's Water Lilies in the Orangerie at the far end. The Musée d'Orsay is across the river by the footbridge. For everything else in Paris, or to fit the Louvre into a longer trip, open the trip planner for France.

Cover photo: King of Hearts, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

faqs.q: Can you see the Louvre in two hours?
faqs.a: You can see its best-known works in two hours if you follow a fixed route through the Sully and Denon wings: the medieval fortress, the Venus de Milo, the Winged Victory, the Mona Lisa and the large French paintings. Nobody sees the whole museum in a day.

faqs.q: Where is the Mona Lisa in the Louvre?
faqs.a: In the Denon wing, on the first floor, in the largest room of the museum. From the Winged Victory at the top of the Daru staircase it is a few minutes on foot, and the way is signposted.

faqs.q: Which entrance to the Louvre is the quickest?
faqs.a: The Carrousel du Louvre entrance, underground, reached from 99 rue de Rivoli or from the metro station, is under cover and often quicker than the Pyramid. Both lead to the same hall, and everyone passes security.

faqs.q: Does a Louvre audio tour include the entry ticket?
faqs.a: Only if the listing says so. Some are sold as ticket plus audio tour, and some are marked "without a ticket", which means commentary only.

faqs.q: Which day is the Louvre closed?
faqs.a: The Louvre is closed on Tuesdays. Opening hours and late evenings change, so check the current ones before your visit.

title: The Acropolis in summer: what time to go up, and what your ticket covers now
subtitle: A bare rock, no shade, a gate that can close at noon, and a combined ticket that no longer exists.
excerpt: When to climb the Acropolis of Athens in the hot months, which entrance to use, what the ticket covers on the rock and its slopes, and what it does not: the museum and the other ancient sites.
focus_keyword: best time to visit the Acropolis in summer
longtail_phrases: what time should I visit the Acropolis in summer
is there still a combined ticket for the Acropolis
does the Acropolis ticket include the Acropolis Museum
which entrance to the Acropolis is less crowded
does the Acropolis close in a heatwave
meta_title: Acropolis in summer: when to go up, what the ticket covers
meta_description: When to climb the Acropolis in the heat, which entrance to use, what the ticket covers and what it does not, now that the combined ticket is gone.

featured_image.alt: The Acropolis of Athens with the Parthenon on top, seen from Philopappos Hill

content_html:
[place attraction="acropolis-of-athens" city="athens"]

For more than two thousand years the Parthenon stood almost whole. It had been a temple of Athena, then a church, then a mosque, and it still had its roof. On the evening of 26 September 1687 a Venetian army was besieging the Ottoman garrison on the Acropolis, and the garrison was keeping its gunpowder inside the building. A mortar shell came through the roof. The explosion blew out the middle of the temple and killed some three hundred people.

What you climb up to see is the ruin that one evening left, patiently put back together since. And because it stands on a bare limestone rock 150 metres above sea level, in a city where July afternoons pass 35 degrees, the first question about a summer visit is not which ticket. It is what time.

What time to go up

There is almost no shade on the Acropolis, and the pale marble throws the light and the heat back at you. Two windows work in summer:

  • The first entry of the day. The gates open at eight. For about an hour the rock is cool and half empty, before the coaches and the cruise ship groups arrive, which they do between nine and noon.
  • The last two hours. In high summer the site stays open into the evening. The heat has dropped, the groups have gone and the low sun turns the marble the colour of honey. Give yourself at least ninety minutes before closing.

Avoid eleven to five. This is not only about comfort: during heatwaves the Greek Ministry of Culture closes the Acropolis through the hottest hours, sometimes from noon until late afternoon, and announces it a day ahead or on the morning itself. If your ticket is for early afternoon in July or August, look at the news before you set off.

The Propylaia, the gateway everybody passes through. Note the bare rock and the absence of shade. Photo: Jakub Hałun, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

Which entrance

Entry is sold by time slot, and there are two gates.

  • The main entrance, on the west side, is where the coaches unload. It is the shortest way to the top and the busiest.
  • The side entrance, at the south-east corner, is five minutes from the metro station Akropoli (line 2) and usually much quieter. From here the path climbs the south slope past the Theatre of Dionysus, so you see more on the way up.

What the ticket covers, and what it does not

Older guidebooks, and plenty of websites, still describe a combined ticket that covered the Acropolis and six other ancient sites of Athens over five days. It was withdrawn in April 2025. Each site now has its own ticket, so plan on that basis.

A ticket for the Acropolis covers the rock and both of its slopes:

  • The Propylaia, the monumental gateway of the 430s BC that every visitor walks through, with the small temple of Athena Nike perched beside it.
  • The Parthenon, built between 447 and 432 BC, when Pericles led Athens. You walk around it; nobody goes inside.
  • The Erechtheion, with its porch held up by six statues of women. The ones on the building are copies. Five of the originals are in the Acropolis Museum and the sixth is in the British Museum in London.
  • The south slope: the Theatre of Dionysus, where the plays of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides were first staged, and the view down into the Odeon of Herodes Atticus, a Roman concert hall of the second century.

The Parthenon. You walk around it, not into it. Photo: Jebulon, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

The porch of the Erechtheion. The six figures on the building are copies. Photo: Coolcaesar, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

It does not cover the Acropolis Museum, the modern building at the foot of the rock where the original sculptures are kept. The museum is a separate institution with its own ticket and its own hours. Nor does it cover the Ancient Agora, the Roman Agora, Hadrian's Library, the Temple of Olympian Zeus or the Kerameikos cemetery.

Reading the partner's listings

Three kinds of product carry the word Acropolis, and they are not interchangeable.

  • A ticket with an audio tour includes entry to the Acropolis and a guide that plays in the partner's app, on the rock and on a walk through the old city afterwards.
  • A listing named for the Acropolis Museum. The museum and the rock are two different places with two different tickets. Open the "included" section and make sure the one written there is the one you want.
  • Self-guided audio walks are the cheapest and the most numerous. They are commentary only: you buy your entry separately. With your own ticket in hand they are a good way to make sense of the ruins, since there is very little explanation on the site itself.

These are the Acropolis tickets and audio tours our partner sells, with today's prices:

[partner attraction="acropolis-of-athens" match="acropolis" limit="6"]

On the rock

  • Wear shoes with grip. Centuries of feet have polished the marble underfoot and it is slippery even when dry.
  • Bring water, a hat and sunscreen. There is nothing to buy beyond the gates.
  • Large bags are not allowed up; there is a cloakroom at the entrance.
  • Do not touch the marble or pick up stones. The guards whistle, often.
  • Allow an hour and a half to two hours, slopes included.

Opening hours shorten step by step from September and some days of the year are free, which makes them the most crowded. The current hours are on our page for the Acropolis of Athens.

The Theatre of Dionysus, on the south slope, inside the same ticket. Photo: Jakub Hałun, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

From here

Keep the hot middle of the day for the Acropolis Museum, which is air-conditioned and three hundred metres from the side entrance. Beside the main entrance, the bare rock of the Areopagus is free to climb and looks over the Ancient Agora. Below the north slope are the lanes of Plaka and the whitewashed houses of Anafiotika. At sunset, walk up Philopappos Hill, where the cover photo of this guide was taken. See what else Athens has close by, or open the attractions map of Greece if the city is the start of a longer trip.

Cover photo: Jakub Hałun, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit the Acropolis in summer?
faqs.a: The first entry at eight in the morning, before the tour groups arrive, or the last two hours before closing, when it is cooler and the light is softer. Avoid the hours between eleven and five.

faqs.q: Is there still a combined ticket for the Acropolis and other sites in Athens?
faqs.a: No. The combined ticket for the Acropolis and six other ancient sites was withdrawn in April 2025. Each site now has its own ticket.

faqs.q: Does the Acropolis ticket include the Acropolis Museum?
faqs.a: No. The ticket covers the rock and its two slopes, including the Theatre of Dionysus. The Acropolis Museum is a separate institution with its own ticket.

faqs.q: Does the Acropolis close when it is very hot?
faqs.a: It can. During heatwaves the Greek Ministry of Culture closes the site through the hottest hours of the day, at short notice. Check the news on the day if your slot is around midday.

faqs.q: How long does a visit to the Acropolis take?
faqs.a: About an hour and a half to two hours for the monuments on top and the south slope. Add at least an hour and a half if you also visit the Acropolis Museum.

title: Prague Castle: what is free, and what needs a ticket
subtitle: The courtyards cost nothing. The four interiors that matter are behind one ticket. Here is the difference.
excerpt: Prague Castle is a walled district, not one building. What you can see without paying, what the standard ticket opens, what is sold separately, and how to walk it in half a day.
longtail_phrases: is Prague Castle free to enter
what does the Prague Castle ticket include
do you need a ticket for St Vitus Cathedral
is Golden Lane free in the evening
how long does it take to visit Prague Castle
meta_title: Prague Castle: what is free and what needs a ticket
meta_description: The courtyards and gardens of Prague Castle are free. What the ticket opens, what is sold separately, and how to see the castle in half a day.

featured_image.alt: Prague Castle and the spires of St Vitus Cathedral above the roofs of the Lesser Town, seen across the Vltava

content_html:
[place attraction="prague-castle" city="prague"]

On 23 May 1618 a crowd of Protestant noblemen pushed into the offices of the Bohemian Chancellery at Prague Castle, held a short and angry trial of two of the emperor's Catholic governors, and threw both of them out of the window. Their secretary followed. The drop into the castle ditch was some twenty metres, and all three lived. Catholics said angels had caught them. Protestants said they had landed in a heap of dung.

The Thirty Years' War began with that fall, and the window is still there, in the Old Royal Palace. Whether you can stand at it depends on a question visitors rarely ask before they are at the gate: which parts of this castle are free, and which need a ticket?

A castle that is really a district

Prague Castle is not one building. Founded around 880, it grew into a walled hilltop about 570 metres long holding a cathedral, a basilica, a convent, several palaces, three courtyards, a street of tiny houses and gardens on every side. It is also where the president of the Czech Republic has his office.

That is why there is no ticket "for the castle". You walk into the grounds free of charge, through a security check at the gate, and you pay only to go inside certain buildings.

The second courtyard: free to walk through, like all the courtyards. Photo: Tilman2007, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

What you can see without a ticket

  • The courtyards and lanes, from early morning until late evening, long after the interiors have closed.
  • The outside of St Vitus Cathedral, including the south side with its fourteenth-century mosaic of the Last Judgment over the Golden Gate. Without a ticket you get, at most, a look into the nave from just inside the west door.
  • The changing of the guard. Sentries change on the hour at the gates. The full ceremony, with a fanfare and an exchange of flags, is at noon in the first courtyard.
  • The gardens, in the warm months: the Royal Garden to the north and the South Gardens along the ramparts, with the classic view over the red roofs of the Lesser Town. They are closed in winter.
  • Golden Lane after hours. The lane has usually been left open, free, once its houses close for the day. You see the street and not the interiors. Ask on the day whether this still applies.

What the ticket opens

The standard ticket, which the castle calls the main circuit, opens four interiors. It has been valid for two days, each interior once.

  • St Vitus Cathedral. Begun in 1344 under Charles IV and finished only in 1929. Inside the ticket barrier are the stained glass, including the window Alfons Mucha painted in 1931, the silver tomb of St John of Nepomuk, and the Chapel of St Wenceslas, its walls set with polished stones. A door in that chapel, with seven locks, leads to the chamber where the Bohemian crown jewels are kept.
  • The Old Royal Palace. The Vladislav Hall, completed in 1502, is 62 metres long under a single vault and was big enough for indoor tournaments: the knights rode up a staircase built for horses. The window of 1618 is in a room off the hall.
  • St George's Basilica. Behind a red baroque front stands the oldest church interior at the castle, founded around 920: plain stone, round arches, and the tombs of early Bohemian princes.
  • Golden Lane. A row of very small houses built against the castle wall at the end of the sixteenth century for the castle guards. Franz Kafka wrote in number 22 through the winter of 1916 to 1917.

The vault of the Vladislav Hall, finished in 1502. Photo: Interfase, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

St George's Basilica: a red baroque front on a church of the tenth century. Photo: Dennis G. Jarvis, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.

Sold separately, and not part of that ticket: the climb up the cathedral's Great South Tower, the castle's permanent exhibitions such as the Picture Gallery, and the Lobkowicz Palace, which is privately owned and runs its own ticket desk.

Reading the partner's listings

  • A castle ticket is entry to the interiors. Check which buildings are named, for how many days it is valid, and whether you have to collect or exchange anything on the spot.
  • A ticket with an audio tour or a mobile guide adds commentary on your own phone. One listing also starts with a short orientation by a person, which is not a guided tour.
  • An audio tour of the castle with no ticket is the cheapest option and works well for the free parts: it tells the stories of the courtyards and the exteriors. To go inside you still need an entry ticket.

"Skip the line" here means you do not queue at the ticket office. The security check at the gate and the line at the cathedral door are the same for everyone.

These are the Prague Castle tickets and audio tours our partner sells, with today's prices:

[partner attraction="prague-castle" match="castle" limit="6"]

How to walk it in half a day

  • Arrive from above. Take tram 22 up the hill to the stop Pražský hrad and walk in on the level, then leave downhill. Climbing from the river first costs you twenty minutes and your legs.
  • Cathedral first. It has the longest line, and it closes to visitors during services, which on Sundays means the whole morning. Be at the door when the interiors open.
  • Then east, downhill: the Old Royal Palace, St George's Basilica, Golden Lane. The ticket barriers follow that order.

Allow three hours with the four interiors, or an hour for the free parts alone. The buildings close earlier in winter than in summer; the current hours are on our page for Prague Castle, and St Vitus Cathedral has a page of its own.

Golden Lane: houses built into the castle wall for its guards. Photo: Diego Delso, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

From here

Leave by the eastern gate beyond Golden Lane and take the Old Castle Stairs down to the metro at Malostranská, or go out by the main gate and walk down Nerudova street through the Lesser Town to Charles Bridge, twenty minutes away and downhill all the way. Uphill from the castle, the Strahov Monastery has two painted library halls. For the rest of Prague, or a longer route through the country, open the trip planner for Czechia.

Cover photo: Mgimelfarb, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: Is Prague Castle free to enter?
faqs.a: The grounds are. You can walk through the courtyards, see the cathedral from outside, watch the changing of the guard and, in the warm months, visit the gardens without a ticket. A ticket is needed to go inside the historic buildings.

faqs.q: What does the Prague Castle ticket include?
faqs.a: The standard ticket, the main circuit, opens four interiors: St Vitus Cathedral, the Old Royal Palace, St George's Basilica and Golden Lane. The cathedral tower and the permanent exhibitions are sold separately.

faqs.q: Do you need a ticket for St Vitus Cathedral?
faqs.a: Yes, to walk through it. Without a ticket you can see the outside and, at most, look into the nave from just inside the west door. The chapels and the stained glass are beyond the ticket barrier.

faqs.q: When is the changing of the guard at Prague Castle?
faqs.a: The sentries at the gates change every hour. The full ceremony, with a fanfare and an exchange of flags, takes place at noon in the first courtyard. It is free to watch.

faqs.q: How long does it take to visit Prague Castle?
faqs.a: About three hours with the four interiors of the standard ticket. The free parts, the courtyards and the views, take around an hour.

title: Doge's Palace: what the ticket includes, and how to cross the Bridge of Sighs
subtitle: The bridge and the prisons are in every ticket. St Mark's Basilica and the secret rooms are not.
excerpt: What an ordinary Doge's Palace ticket covers in Venice, how you get onto the Bridge of Sighs, what the Secret Itineraries tour adds, and what is never included.

featured_image.alt: The pink and white waterfront façade of the Doge's Palace in Venice, with its two tiers of arcades

content_html:
[place attraction="doge-s-palace" city="venice"]

High on the walls of the largest room in the Doge's Palace runs a row of portraits: the first seventy-six doges of Venice, one after another. One frame holds no face. It shows a painted black cloth and a line of Latin: this is the place of Marino Faliero, beheaded for his crimes. Faliero was elected doge in 1354. Within months he was plotting to do away with the councils of nobles and rule as a prince. He was found out, tried in this building, and beheaded on its stairs in April 1355.

The palace was built for that purpose: to house the head of the Republic and to keep an eye on him. It was a residence, a parliament, a law court and a prison under one roof, which is why a visit here is longer and stranger than people expect, and why it helps to know what your ticket opens.

The Giants' Staircase, where a new doge was crowned in sight of everyone. Photo: Dennis G. Jarvis, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.

What an ordinary ticket covers

The standard ticket for the palace is in fact a ticket for the museums of St Mark's Square. It covers:

  • The Doge's Palace, on a one-way route: the courtyard, the Golden Staircase, the doge's apartments, the council rooms, the armoury, the Bridge of Sighs and the prisons.
  • The Correr Museum, at the opposite end of the square, with the Archaeological Museum and the monumental rooms of the Marciana Library, which are reached through it. Most visitors never use this half of their ticket.

Three rooms on the way are worth slowing down for. The Golden Staircase, its vault thick with gilded stucco, was the ceremonial way up for ambassadors. The Chamber of the Great Council, 53 metres long with not a single column, held the whole voting nobility of Venice: more than a thousand men at a sitting. The wall behind the doge's seat is filled by Tintoretto's Paradise, about 22 metres across, one of the largest paintings on canvas anywhere. And all along the route you pass the stone lions' mouths, letter boxes into which citizens could drop written accusations.

The Chamber of the Great Council, with no column to hold up the ceiling. Photo: Zairon, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

How you cross the Bridge of Sighs

There are two ways to meet the bridge, and they are easily confused.

From the outside, you look at it. The place is the Ponte della Paglia, the bridge on the waterfront a few steps east of the palace. It is free and crowded all day.

From the inside, you walk through it, and the only way to do that is to visit the palace. The Bridge of Sighs is part of the ordinary route: it needs no special ticket. Built around 1600, it links the courtrooms to the New Prisons across the canal. Inside it is a narrow corridor of stone, divided lengthwise in two, with small grilled windows giving onto the lagoon. The name comes from the idea that a condemned man sighed here at his last sight of Venice. Lord Byron made it famous two centuries later. You cross one way, walk through the cells, and come back along the other corridor.

The Bridge of Sighs from the outside, which costs nothing. Photo: kallerna, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

What the Secret Itineraries tour adds

The Secret Itineraries is a separate visit: a guided tour, in a small group, at a fixed time and in a set language, through rooms that are closed to the ordinary ticket. It lasts about an hour and a quarter and is sold in limited numbers, so in season it sells out well ahead.

It takes you behind the state rooms, into the cramped wooden offices where the Republic's clerks worked, the chamber where suspects were questioned, and up under the roof to the Piombi, the cells beneath the lead roofing. Giacomo Casanova was locked up there in 1755 and got out through the roof fifteen months later. Afterwards you are free to follow the ordinary route alone, so nothing is lost.

Take it if the machinery of the state interests you more than the paintings do, and if steep, narrow stairs are not a problem. With small children or little time, the ordinary route is enough: it already includes the bridge and the prisons.

The prisons, at the far end of the ordinary route. Photo: Ethan Doyle White, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

What is not included

  • St Mark's Basilica. It stands against the palace, but it is a church with its own entrance, its own ticket and its own line. No palace ticket lets you in.
  • The Campanile, the bell tower in the square, also separate.
  • The city's access fee. On certain busy days Venice asks day visitors to register and pay a contribution to enter the old city. It has nothing to do with museum tickets.

Reading the partner's listings

  • A fast track ticket is entry to the palace without queuing at the ticket office. Everybody still passes the security check.
  • A ticket with an audio tour adds a guide in the partner's app on your phone, for the palace and for a walk around the square outside. The basilica is described from outside; entry to it is not part of the product.
  • An audio tour marked "without tickets" is commentary only. You buy your entry to the palace yourself.
  • If the Secret Itineraries is what you want, look for those words in the title and in the "included" section. A plain or fast track ticket does not cover it.

These are the Doge's Palace tickets and audio tours our partner sells, with today's prices:

[partner attraction="doge-s-palace" match="doge" limit="6"]

Practical notes

  • Visitors enter by the Porta del Frumento, on the waterfront side, not from the square. The way out is through the courtyard and the carved Gothic gate beside the basilica, the Porta della Carta.
  • Allow an hour and a half to two hours for the palace. There are many stairs; ask about the lift at the entrance if you need it.
  • Backpacks and large bags go to the cloakroom.
  • The nearest vaporetto stop is San Zaccaria.

Opening hours change with the season. The current ones are on our page for the Doge's Palace.

From here

St Mark's Basilica is next door, and the other half of your ticket, the Correr Museum, waits across the square with a fraction of the crowd. Then walk east along the Riva degli Schiavoni, where the tour groups thin out within five minutes. See what else there is to do in Venice, or open the attractions map of Italy if the city is one stop of several.

Cover photo: kallerna, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: Can you walk across the Bridge of Sighs?
faqs.a: Yes, but only from inside the Doge's Palace. The bridge is part of the ordinary visitor route and needs no special ticket. From the outside you can look at it for free from the Ponte della Paglia.

faqs.q: What does a Doge's Palace ticket include?
faqs.a: The palace on its full route, with the council rooms, the armoury, the Bridge of Sighs and the prisons, and also the Correr Museum, the Archaeological Museum and the monumental rooms of the Marciana Library on St Mark's Square.

faqs.q: Does the Doge's Palace ticket include St Mark's Basilica?
faqs.a: No. The basilica is a separate visit with its own entrance, ticket and line. The bell tower is separate as well.

faqs.q: What is the Secret Itineraries tour?
faqs.a: A guided tour in a small group, at a fixed time, through rooms closed to the ordinary ticket: the offices of the state, the interrogation chamber and the cells under the roof where Casanova was held. It is booked separately and sells out early in season.

faqs.q: How long does a visit to the Doge's Palace take?
faqs.a: An hour and a half to two hours for the ordinary route. Add about an hour and a quarter for the Secret Itineraries tour, after which you can continue through the palace on your own.
